summary: Defines how Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (FCIP) entities can be found using the Service Location Protocol version 2 (SLPv2). It specifies the service information that FCIP devices advertise so peers can locate them without manual configuration.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3822 shows how Fibre Channel over TCP/IP endpoints are found with the Service Location Protocol version 2. It defines the template that describes such an endpoint, and a way for an administrator to say which endpoints are allowed to discover which others.

questions: what is an fcip discovery domain
how do fcip entities find each other
subtitle: How Fibre Channel over TCP/IP endpoints find each other with the Service Location Protocol.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel over TCP/IP endpoints need to find one another before they can connect, and the addresses are rarely known in advance. Without a way to discover them, every link has to be configured by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the service type templates an FCIP entity registers with the Service Location Protocol, plus a discovery domain attribute that lets an administrator control which entities can find which.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3822 is a Proposed Standard from July 2004 and has been updated by RFC 7146.

today: RFC 3822 is a Proposed Standard from July 2004 and has been updated by RFC 7146. Its service type template service:fcip:entity is the registered way for Fibre Channel over TCP/IP endpoints to advertise themselves for discovery.

sections.title: What the Document Covers
sections.content:
The RFC describes the use of the Service Location Protocol version 2 to perform dynamic discovery of participating Fibre Channel over TCP/IP entities. It specifies implementation guidelines, service type templates and security considerations.

The scope is narrow on purpose. It covers how FCIP entities are advertised and found; it does not change how they connect, which is defined in RFC 3821.
sections.plainLanguage: The document covers discovery only: how an endpoint advertises itself, how another endpoint finds it, and how an administrator limits who may find whom.

sections.title: The Terms Used
sections.content:
Some definitions are reproduced from the SLP and FCIP specifications. A User Agent is a process working on the client's behalf to establish contact with some service; it retrieves service information from the Service Agents or Directory Agents. A Service Agent is a process working on behalf of one or more services to advertise the services and their capabilities. A Directory Agent is a process that collects service advertisements, and there can be only one on a given host.

A Scope is a named set of services, typically making up a logical administrative group. A Service Advertisement is a URL, attributes and a lifetime, which says how long the advertisement is valid, and it provides the service access information and a capabilities description for a particular service.

An FCIP Entity is the principal FCIP interface point to the IP network. Its FCIP Entity Name is the worldwide name of the switch if the entity resides in a switch, or the worldwide node name of the associated Nx_Port. An FCIP Discovery Domain specifies which FCIP entities are allowed to discover each other within the bounds of the scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Three SLP roles appear throughout: the service agent advertises, the user agent asks, and the directory agent collects the advertisements. An FCIP entity is one endpoint of the protocol, and it has a name and a set of discovery domains.

sections.title: How Discovery Works
sections.content:
At least two FCIP entities must be involved, and the end result is that one entity discovers one or more peer entities. Each FCIP entity contains an FCIP control and services module that interfaces to an SLP service agent and user agent.

The service agent builds a service advertisement of the type service:fcip:entity for each of the service URLs it wishes to register, and the advertisement contains a lifetime along with the other attributes defined in the service template.

The rest of the discovery process is the same as for any client and server pair implementing SLPv2. If a directory agent is found, the service agent contacts it and registers the service advertisement. Whether or not a directory agent is found, the service agent keeps the advertisement itself and answers multicast user agent queries directly. When the FCIP entity needs contact information for a peer, the user agent either contacts the directory agent by unicast or the service agent by multicast, using an SLP service request. That request includes a query, based on the attributes, that says what characteristics the peer entities it requires must have. Once the user agent has the IP address and port number of a peer FCIP entity, it may begin the normal connection procedure described in RFC 3821.

The RFC recommends the use of a directory agent for SLPv2 operations in an FCIP environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint advertises itself as a service of type service:fcip:entity, with a lifetime and a set of attributes. Another endpoint asks for the peers it needs, either through a directory agent or by a multicast query, and then connects in the ordinary way.

sections.title: FCIP Discovery Domains
sections.content:
A discovery domain gives finer control over which FCIP entities may discover each other inside a specific SLP scope. The example uses the scope fcip and three domains. The domain purple allows entities A, B and C to discover each other. The domain orange allows entity A to discover entity B but not entity C. The domain blue allows entity C to discover entity B but not entity A.

With that arrangement, the value of the fcip-discovery-domain attribute is orange,purple for entity A, orange,blue,purple for entity B, and blue,purple for entity C. A user agent searching for all entities in a named domain therefore only finds the peers that share that domain with it.
sections.plainLanguage: A discovery domain is a label that entities share. Two endpoints can find each other only if they have a domain in common, so the administrator can permit some pairs and forbid others inside one SLP scope.

sections.title: The Service Type Templates
sections.content:
Two templates are provided. The FCIP abstract service type template defines the abstract service service:fcip, used as a top-level service to encapsulate all other FCIP related services. Its URL syntax leaves the path to depend on the concrete service type, and its template version is 0.1.

The FCIP entity concrete service type template defines the service service:fcip:entity. A device holding FCIP entities that wants them discovered through SLPv2 registers each of them with each of its addresses under this service type. The template version is again 0.1, and the URL syntax is a host, optionally followed by a colon and a port. The RFC notes that a DNS host name should be used along with the well-known IANA FCIP port number when working with NAT or NAPT devices, and gives the examples service:fcip:entity://host.example.com and service:fcip:entity://192.0.2.0:4000.

The template defines four attributes. fcip-entity-name is an opaque string: if the entity is a VE_Port or B_Access implementation residing in a switch, the name is the Fibre Channel switch name, and otherwise it is the Fibre Channel node name of the associated port, such as an Nx_Port. An entity that represents multiple endpoints must register each endpoint separately. transports is a list of the transport protocols the registered entity supports, and FCIP is currently supported over TCP only. mgmt-entity holds the URLs of the management interfaces, appropriate for SNMP, web-based or telnet management, with examples such as http://fcipentity.example.com:1080/ and telnet://fcipentity.example.com. fcip-discovery-domain holds the names of the discovery domains the entity belongs to.

The RFC gives three example query strings. To find a specific entity, the query is on the FCIP entity name, in the scope fcip-entity-scope-list. To find all entities in a given discovery domain, the query is on the discovery domain name. A management application that wants every entity uses no query at all, in the scope management-service-scope-list.
sections.plainLanguage: The template says how to write the service URL and gives four attributes: the name of the endpoint, the transports it speaks, the addresses of its management interface, and the discovery domains it belongs to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The SLPv2 security model does not provide confidentiality, but it does provide a way for user agents to be sure that service advertisements come only from trusted service agents, except that it offers no way to authenticate a response that returns no results.

Once an FCIP entity has been discovered, authentication and authorisation are handled by the FCIP protocol itself. It is the responsibility of the providers of those services to make sure that an inappropriately advertised or discovered service does not compromise their security.

Without security in SLPv2, there is a risk that false discovery information is distributed. The main countermeasure is authentication. Where that risk matters, IPsec security associations should be used for FCIP traffic so that it only flows between endpoints that took part in IKE authentication. An attacker who distributes discovery information claiming to be an FCIP endpoint will lack the secrets needed to complete IKE authentication, and so will be prevented from sending or receiving FCIP traffic falsely.

A denial of service risk remains, based on repeated use of false discovery information that triggers IKE negotiation. The countermeasures are administrative configuration of each FCIP entity to limit the peers it will talk to, by IP address range or DNS domain, and a negative authentication cache that avoids repeatedly contacting an entity that fails to authenticate. The RFC states that these three measures must be implemented.

For the implementation, the RFC points to RFC 3723. IPsec is mandatory to implement for the block storage clients and servers, so all of them, including those invoking SLP, can be assumed to support it. SLP servers cannot be assumed to implement it, because standard SLP has no such requirement, and in particular a directory agent may run on a machine that runs no block storage protocol. IPsec should be implemented for SLPv2, including ESP with a non-null transform to provide both authentication and confidentiality. Because the block storage services have their own authentication capabilities once located, SLPv2 authentication is optional to implement and use.
sections.plainLanguage: Discovery alone proves nothing, so the FCIP protocol still authenticates the peer it connects to. The RFC asks for three defences against a flood of false adverts: restrict which peers an endpoint will talk to, cache the failures, and use IPsec.

sections.title: Registration and Internationalization
sections.content:
The two SLP templates described in section 5 should be registered in the IANA SVRLOC Templates registry, following the process in the IANA considerations of RFC 2609.

On internationalization, SLP allows internationalized strings to be registered and retrieved. Attributes in the template that are not marked as literal are registered in a localized manner. An English localization must be registered, and others may be.
sections.plainLanguage: The two templates are registered with IANA in the registry for SLP service templates, and the English wording of the attributes is the required one.

messages.label: Service registration
messages.note: The service agent registers the service:fcip:entity advertisement.

messages.label: Service request
messages.note: The user agent asks for the peers it needs, by attribute query.

messages.label: Service reply
messages.note: Returns the URLs of the matching peers, with their addresses and ports.

messages.label: FCIP connection
messages.note: The normal FCIP connection procedure starts from the address and port found.

THE ATTRIBUTES OF THE service:fcip:entity TEMPLATE

items.title: fcip-entity-name
items.text: The Fibre Channel switch name, or the node name of the associated port.

items.title: transports
items.text: The transport protocols the entity supports. FCIP is currently supported over TCP only.

items.title: mgmt-entity
items.text: The URLs of the management interfaces, for SNMP, web-based or telnet management.

items.title: fcip-discovery-domain
items.text: The names of the discovery domains the entity belongs to, which control who may find it.
